Question 5 of 11 · Is there a Creator?

If God exists, why is there suffering?

Short answer

Suffering doesn’t disprove God. The Quran says this life is a test.

Source: Quran 67:2 (opens in a new tab)

If your doubt comes from real personal pain — loss, grief, injustice — this is not a place for more arguments. What you're carrying deserves a real conversation, not a web page. We'd genuinely love to hear from you.

Talk to us

Objections

What people say against this, and our answer. Open one to read it.

You might say“Bad things happen — how can there be a God?”

Our answer

Evil and suffering are real. But do they disprove God — or do they sharpen the question?

What philosophers and theologians actually argue

The “logical” problem of evil says God and evil cannot both exist. J. L. Mackie stated it in 1955. A famous answer is Alvin Plantinga’s Free Will Defense (1974). The Internet Encyclopedia of Philosophy concludes that “Mackie was wrong to think that it is logically impossible” for “God is omnipotent, omniscient, and perfectly good” and “Evil exists” to both be true.

A world where genuine moral choice is possible must be a world where evil is possible. A God who overrides every bad choice or natural consequence would not have created free beings — he would have created puppets.

ArticleInternet Encyclopedia of Philosophy: The Evidential Problem of Evil↗(opens in a new tab)
Read more

The remaining debate is the "evidential" problem: not that evil disproves God, but that the sheer amount of suffering makes God's existence less probable. This is a serious argument, but it depends on our ability to judge what a perfect God "should" permit — which is itself a huge assumption. It also doesn't address whether the suffering serves purposes we cannot fully see.

You might say“But what about innocent suffering — children, natural disasters?”

Our answer

Innocent suffering is the hardest case. Islam doesn't dismiss it — it answers it directly.

The Islamic answer to innocent suffering

Islam teaches that this life is a test, and that suffering here is not the end of the story. The Quran says:

وَلَنَبْلُوَنَّكُم بِشَيْءٍ مِّنَ الْخَوْفِ وَالْجُوعِ وَنَقْصٍ مِّنَ الْأَمْوَالِ وَالْأَنفُسِ وَالثَّمَرَاتِ ۗ وَبَشِّرِ الصَّابِرِينَ

“We will certainly test you with a touch of fear and famine and loss of property, life, and crops. Give good news to those who patiently endure…”

Quran 2:155

And the Prophet Muhammad ﷺ said: “No fatigue, nor disease, nor sorrow, nor sadness, nor hurt, nor distress befalls a Muslim, even if it were the prick he receives from a thorn, but that Allah expiates some of his sins for that.” Suffering in this life is not pointless: it is a test, and it wipes away sins.

SourceQuran 2:155↗(opens in a new tab)SourceSahih al-Bukhari 5641↗(opens in a new tab)
You might say“Why design a world that needs this much suffering at all?”

Our answer

Could the highest human qualities exist without the possibility of suffering?

Why suffering is the condition for meaning

Courage requires real danger. Compassion requires real pain. Patience requires real hardship. Sacrifice requires something genuinely costly. A world without any possibility of suffering would be a world without any of these — a world of permanent comfort where nothing is at stake and nothing truly matters.

The philosopher John Hick called this “soul-making,” most fully in his 1966 book Evil and the God of Love: this world is not built for comfort but for growth. We are not here as tourists in a hotel. We are here to become something, and that takes resistance.

Islam says this directly. The Quran asks: “Do people think once they say, ‘We believe,’ that they will be left without being put to the test?” (29:2). The test is not a flaw in the design. It is the design.

ArticleInternet Encyclopedia of Philosophy: The Evidential Problem of Evil↗(opens in a new tab)SourceQuran 29:2↗(opens in a new tab)
Read more

The objection assumes the purpose of existence is maximising comfort. But that's a value judgment, not an obvious truth. If the purpose is something deeper — the development of genuine character, the exercise of real freedom, the earning of a place in something eternal — then a world with resistance makes perfect sense. Islam doesn't promise that this life will be easy. It promises that it will be worth it.
